The Quiet Joy of Reading Slowly

By Jane Doe · March 4, 2025

There is a particular pleasure in reading slowly, one that the modern internet seems designed to erase. When we skim, we gather facts; when we linger, we gather meaning. This essay is about the difference between those two activities and why it matters more than ever.

Consider the humble e-reader. Unlike a phone, it offers no notifications, no infinite scroll, and no autoplaying video. It is, in the best sense, boring. And boredom, as Pascal suggested, is where thought begins.

A short history of attention

Historians of reading have long distinguished between intensive and extensive reading. The intensive reader read a few books, over and over; the extensive reader read many books, once. The shift from one to the other in the eighteenth century was, some argue, a revolution comparable to the printing press itself.

“We read to know we are not alone.” — attributed to C.S. Lewis

Today we are extensive readers to a degree our ancestors could not have imagined. The average person encounters tens of thousands of words a day, most of them in fragments. The question is not whether we read, but how.

  • Read on paper or e-ink when you can.
  • Turn off notifications.
  • Finish what you start — or don't, deliberately.

In the end, slow reading is less a technique than a disposition: a willingness to let a text take the time it needs. Café owners and naïve readers alike know this — some things can’t be hurried.
